summary: In this excerpt from Book 6 (part 52) of a fiction story, the first-person narrator stands before a booby-trapped door, weighing the risk of lifting it. She has checked the wiring and magnets, admits she cannot be sure she missed nothing, and recalls a mocking memory of a girl twirling a voltmeter. Despite fear and an inner voice of caution, she hauls the door chain and the door screeches open. Afterward she feels nauseated, her legs weaken, and her left hand burns.
one_line: A narrator risks a possibly explosive door to escape, hauls it open, then suffers nausea and a burning hand.
key_facts: The narrator has more than nineteen minutes left before the deadline when she stands back from the door.
Her wire-wrapped nails are poking up next to the door magnets.
She has four small electromagnets that she checks with her eyes after the door opens.
She thinks of a scrawny dark-skinned girl arrogantly twirling a voltmeter across her fingers, whose laughter echoes in her memory with an edge of maliciousness.
The narrator estimates she is probably not about to get blown up, repeating the word 'Probably.'
She describes a vast net of explosives surrounding her that could blast her into bloody fragments blended with bite-sized concrete.
She tells herself that this is a job like any other and that she always takes risks for jobs.
She notes that she is not even getting paid for the job.
The narrator jokes that if she blew herself up, Arthur would realize he should have appreciated her.
The inner voice of caution or sanity shakes its head in disgust and departs.
She leans her whole body weight on the door chain and hauls, and the door screeches up on its tracks.
A dusty breeze blows in from the alley outside, making the sweat on her face clammy.
The urge to vomit redoubles, her legs want to melt, and her left hand starts burning.
The narrator reflects that her body knew how dumb she was being even when she did not.
